codebook.source: MONK-2 problem (Thrun et al. 1991), PMLB 'monk2' deduplicated to the 432 input configurations; attributes a1-a6 are abstract (no real-world meaning), so statements are phrased in rule terms on the attribute values

sentences.text: This count stage reads all six attributes, a2 only through a small pair gate on a2, a3 and a6. It acts on 290 of 345 training cases, 85 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 2, a6 = 1), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without it to below 1% with it.

How much a1 = 3 instead of 1 moves the prediction depends on a5: for the typical case, it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 9% to about 93% when a5 is not 1, but leaves it below 1% when a5 = 1.
Through it, a1 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 and a5 other than 1 lower the probability and a4 = 1 raises it, all below 1% for the typical case it acts on.

This ramp adds up all six attributes with fixed weights. Through it, a5 = 4 instead of 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%, and a5 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 raises it to about 9%.
Through it, a3 = 2, a1 = 2 or 3, a2 = 2 instead of 3 and a6 = 2 also raise it, and a4 = 1 and a2 = 1 lower it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

lead.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1) the model gives a predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; it adds up two parts, a count stage that pulls 'yes' down for most cases and a ramp in which a5 counts most.

evidence.text: Through it, a2 = 2 instead of 3 takes the typical case from about 3% to about 5% when a3 = 2, and leaves it below 1% when a3 = 1.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

hypothesis.text: This small pair gate reads a2, a3 and a6 and passes them on to the count stage; through it, a2 = 2 instead of 3 raises the probability of 'yes' when a3 = 2.

evidence.text: It reads a1, a3, a4, a5 and a6 directly and a2, a3 and a6 through a small pair gate (explained below), combined in a way that is not a plain sum.

It acts on 290 of 345 training cases, 85 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 2, a6 = 1), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without it to below 1% with it.

How much a1 = 3 instead of 1 moves the prediction depends on a5: for the typical case, it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 9% to about 93% when a5 is not 1, but leaves it below 1% when a5 = 1.
Through it, a1 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 and a5 other than 1 lower the probability and a4 = 1 raises it, all below 1% for the typical case it acts on.
Changing a1 from 1 to 3 also matters more when a6 = 2 (from below 1% to about 2%), when a3 = 2 (from about 3% to about 1%) and when a4 is not 1 (below 1% either way).

hypothesis.text: This count stage pulls the probability of 'yes' down for most cases: for the typical case it acts on, from about 98% without it to below 1% with it.
Through it, a1 = 3 instead of 1 raises the prediction from about 9% to about 93% when a5 is not 1.

evidence.text: Through it, a5 = 4 instead of 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%, and a5 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 raises it to about 9%.
Through it, a3 = 2, a1 = 2 or 3, a2 = 2 instead of 3 and a6 = 2 also raise it, and a4 = 1 and a2 = 1 lower it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.
Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 345 training cases.

hypothesis.text: This ramp adds up all six attributes with fixed weights, and a5 counts most: a5 = 4 instead of 1 raises the typical case's probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%.

evidence.text: It is made up of two parts, the count stage and the attribute ramp (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 345 training cases.

summary.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1) the model gives a predicted probability of 'yes' below 1%; it adds up two parts, a count stage that pulls 'yes' down for most cases and a ramp in which a5 counts most.

This count stage reads all six attributes, a2 only through a small pair gate on a2, a3 and a6. It acts on 290 of 345 training cases, 85 of which are actually 'yes'; for the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 2, a6 = 1), it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without it to below 1% with it.

How much a1 = 3 instead of 1 moves the prediction depends on a5: for the typical case, it takes the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 9% to about 93% when a5 is not 1, but leaves it below 1% when a5 = 1.
Through it, a1 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 and a5 other than 1 lower the probability and a4 = 1 raises it, all below 1% for the typical case it acts on.

This ramp adds up all six attributes with fixed weights. Through it, a5 = 4 instead of 1 raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 49%, and a5 = 2 or 3 instead of 1 raises it to about 9%.
Through it, a3 = 2, a1 = 2 or 3, a2 = 2 instead of 3 and a6 = 2 also raise it, and a4 = 1 and a2 = 1 lower it, though for the typical case it stays below 1%.

titles.ann_25: Pair gate on a2, a3 and a6

worth_checking.flag: attribute values other than the first matter
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the model separates values of a5 and a2 other than the first: through the ramp, a5 = 4 instead of 1 takes the typical case to about 49% but a5 = 2 or 3 only to about 9%, and a2 = 2 instead of 3 raises the predicted probability of 'yes', which the exactly-two rule does not do.

parts.name: weighted_count_peak
parts.original_hypothesis: Root: score = sigmoid(2.236 + Ramp - 0.918 P - 5.804 L). Ramp falls with weighted indicator count (upper edge); L subtracts up to 41.6 when there are 0-1 indicators (lower edge); P adds an extra penalty (0.918 x 0.95..13.4) when >=2 of a2/a3/a6 are first values and, through L, closes the lower edge. Unconnected inputs a4:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 (no enabled edges) have zero effect; a4 and a5 are read only through a4:1, a5:1, a5:4. Evidence: mean output pre-activation by number of first values (432 inputs): -26.9, -15.4, +0.55, -5.4, -13.2, -21.3, -29.7 for 0..6, a peak at two. Positive predictions: 0/24, 9/92 (8 of them a1=1 alone), 87/142, 4/113, 0/61. The peak is imperfect because the indicators are weighted unequally: a4=1 and a5=1 each count almost double, so pairs containing a5 and {a2,a4},{a4,a5} mostly score negative, while a1=1 alone often scores positive. Train (n=345): accuracy 0.855, AUC 0.946; agreement with the MONK-2 rule on all 432 inputs 0.843. Train sensitivity of output: L 0.31, Ramp 0.053, P 0.049.

parts.name: count_stage
parts.original_hypothesis: Serial composition: pair gate P feeds the low-count gate L (node 584); outputs (P, L). L = ReLU(1.308 + 5.043[a1=2] + 5.853[a1=3] - 1.583[a3=1] - 5.530[a4=1] - 5.532[a5=1] - 0.603[a6=1] - 1.885 P) ~= ReLU(6.7 - 5.4[a1=1] - 5.53[a4=1] - 5.53[a5=1] - 1.58[a3=1] - 0.60[a6=1] - 1.885 P). L is a 'too few indicators' detector: large (up to 7.16) when none of a1=1, a4=1, a5=1 hold and P is quiet; closed by a first value of a1/a4/a5 plus any further indicator, or by P (the P -> L inhibition routes a2/a3/a6 count evidence into the lower edge). Evidence: over all 432 inputs, L>0 for 100% of inputs with 0 or 1 first values (means 6.76, 4.04), 30% with exactly 2 (mean 0.22; L stays ~1.2-1.3 for pairs {a1,a2}, {a2,a4}, {a2,a5}), 0% with >=3. Train sensitivity of L: a1:3 0.96, a4:1 0.90, a5:1 0.85, a1:2 0.84, a3:1 0.28, others <=0.23. Local train ablation: P=0 everywhere -> acc 0.672 / AUC 0.614; L removed -> 0.667 / 0.632 (full 0.855 / 0.946).

parts.name: pair_gate_a2a3a6
parts.original_hypothesis: Pair gate over a2=1, a3=1, a6=1. P = ReLU(0.628 + 2.96 z(a2:1) - 2.11 z(a2:3) + 3.11 z(a3:1) - 4.21 z(a6:2)) = ReLU(-7.469 + 6.26[a2=1] + 6.22[a3=1] + 8.42[a6=1] - 4.44[a2=3]). Evidence (closed form; exhaustive enumeration of the 12 (a2,a3,a6) patterns): all three indicators -> 13.43; two -> 7.22 (a2,a6), 7.17 (a3,a6), 5.01 (a2,a3), 2.73 (a3,a6 with a2=3); one -> 0 except a6=1 alone with a2=2 -> 0.95; none -> 0. So P is a graded at-least-two-of-three counter over the indicators of a2, a3, a6. Train sensitivity is largest for a6:2 (2.17), then a3:1 (1.60), a2:1 (1.53), a2:3 (1.09). It supplies count information for a2 and a6, which the direct linear path barely weighs.

parts.name: linear_count_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: Decreasing weighted linear count ramp (direct input->output connections). Per attribute value: a1: =1 -2.97, =2 +1.27, =3 +2.01; a2: =1 -0.74, =2 +1.17, =3 -0.38; a3: =1 -2.66, =2 +2.80; a4: =1 -5.52, =2/3 +2.48; a5: =1 -7.42, =2/3 +1.74, =4 +4.03; a6: =1 -0.27, =2 +0.29. Each first-value indicator lowers the sum by an unequal amount: a5 (9.2-11.4) and a4 (8.0) count heavily, a3 (5.5) and a1 (4.2-5.0) moderately, a2 (0.4-1.9) and a6 (0.56) barely. Evidence (closed form; enumeration of 432 inputs): ramp + output bias averages 12.3, 8.1, 3.6, -1.1, -6.2, -11.6, -17.3 for 0..6 first values (range -17.3 to 15.0). It is the upper edge of the response peak. Alone (with bias) it gives train accuracy 0.565, AUC 0.602.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

For a typical case it acts on, it clearly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 98% without this part to below 1% with it.
